paper_metadata.title: Timing, Outcome, and Risk Factors of Intracranial Hemorrhage in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome Patients During Venovenous Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a large, well-defined cohort from a single ARDS referral center with clear inclusion/exclusion criteria and high participation (only 35/479 excluded). Baseline characteristics are thoroughly reported.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: ARDS referral center of the Department of Anesthesiology and Intensive Care Medicine, Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Campus Virchow-Klinikum, Berlin
items.reasoning: The setting and population (ARDS patients requiring ECMO) are clearly defined.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: All adult patients who fulfilled the criteria of the Berlin Definition for ARDS (10) and who were treated with ECMO were eligible for the study.
items.reasoning: The study uses a consecutive cohort from a specific clinical registry, minimizing selection bias.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: between January 2007 and December 2018
items.reasoning: The 11-year recruitment window is explicitly stated.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Campus Virchow-Klinikum, Berlin, between January 2007 and December 2018
items.reasoning: Specific hospital and city are provided.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Patients were excluded if they: 1) had ICH before ECMO initiation, 2) received venoarterial ECMO, 3) were converted from venovenous to venovenous arterial ECMO... 4) had incomplete datasets
items.reasoning: Criteria are explicit and clinical relevant to the prognostic question.

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: A total of 479 ARDS patients with ECMO were identified. Of those, 35 patients were excluded, so that a total of 444 patients with VV-ECMO were eligible for analysis
items.reasoning: Participation rate is >90%, which is excellent for limiting selection bias.

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Baseline characteristics of patients without and with ICH are shown in Table E2... age, gender, comorbidities, admissions scores, ARDS severity, ARDS etiology
items.reasoning: Comprehensive baseline data is provided in the text and supplementary tables.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study is retrospective with very few exclusions for missing data (only 35 total exclusions including clinical reasons). The primary outcome (60-day mortality) is robustly captured via hospital records.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: 444 patients with VV-ECMO were eligible for analysis
items.reasoning: The vast majority of the identified cohort was analyzed.

items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: As a retrospective study using electronic records, 'drop out' is less applicable than in prospective trials, but the text doesn't explicitly discuss tracking patients who might have been transferred out.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factor (ICH) was defined using standard radiological criteria and assessed by experts. While not all patients had routine scans, a high percentage (73.4%) of the control group was scanned, reducing the risk of misclassification.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: defined as occurrence of parenchymal hemorrhage, nonaneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), or subdural hematoma (SDH).
items.reasoning: The prognostic factor (ICH) is clearly defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: All ICHs were diagnosed by an expert neuroradiologist.
items.reasoning: Diagnosis by a specialist using CT imaging is the gold standard.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: Clinical cutoffs of risk factors were identified using a gray zone approach (13).
items.reasoning: The study uses data-driven methods (Youden index/Gray zone) to find cutoffs, which is appropriate for exploration but can be data-dependent.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: A follow-up CCT scan was performed if a new neurologic symptom was observed... 73.4%... of the patients that were classified as patients without evidence for an ICH had a CCT scan
items.reasoning: Not all patients received the same frequency of imaging; some were scanned based on symptoms, others incidentally.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: 444 patients with VV-ECMO were eligible for analysis
items.reasoning: The PF (ICH) was determined for the entire analyzed cohort.

items.reasoning: Imputation was not mentioned; patients with incomplete datasets were excluded.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The outcome (60-day mortality) is objective and clearly defined, leaving little room for measurement bias.

items.reasoning: Mortality at a specific time point is a clear, standard outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The authors adjusted for the RESP score and septic shock, which are major confounders. However, in a retrospective study, unmeasured confounders (e.g., specific anticoagulation nuances or provider-level variations over 11 years) may still exist.

items.reasoning: The RESP score covers most critical prognostic factors in this population.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.evidence_snippet: After adjusting for septic shock and RESP score variables, ICH was independently associated with a three-fold increased chance for death
items.reasoning: Multivariable logistic regression was used to adjust for key prognostic scores.

items.evidence_snippet: multivariable logistic regression was performed using a backward variable selection procedure based on the Akaike information criterion (AIC).
items.reasoning: The strategy is well-described and standard for this type of study.

items.evidence_snippet: Baseline characteristics and variables of interest that were different in univariable analysis were included, as appropriate.
items.reasoning: The model building followed a logical progression from univariable to multivariable analysis.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: multivariable logistic regression... Internal validation of the models demonstrated a good discrimination
items.reasoning: Logistic regression is appropriate for binary outcomes like mortality.
